newsitem.title: USA: Mortgage rates rose in week.
newsitem.headline: Mortgage rates rose in week.

text.p: The average rate on 30-year fixed rate mortgages rose to 7.94 percent in the week ended March 21, the highest level since early October 1996, Freddie Mac said Thursday.
The average rate was 7.84 percent in the previous week.
For 15-year fixed-rate loans, the rate rose to 7.45 percent in the latest week from 7.34 percent in the prior week.
Both the 30- and 15-year loan rates were the highest since the week ended Oct 4, 1996, when the 30-year was at 8.06 percent, and the 15-year at 7.58 percent.

The average commitment rate for one-year adjustable-rate mortgages rose to 5.71 percent in the week, the highest level since 5.82 percent in the week ended Sept 27, 1996. The rate rose from 5.61 percent in the previous week.
A year ago, the 30-year loan rate averaged 7.81 percent, the 15-year 7.32 percent and the ARM 5.60 percent.
Freddie Mac Chief Economist Robert Van Order said rates rose this week in part because of concern that the Federal Reserve was set to raise interest rates when it meets on Tuesday next week.
"Continued concern in the financial markets about the Federal Reserve raising their rates and also some nervousness about inflation led to the rise in rates this week," Van Order said.

Lenders charged an average 1.8 percent in fees and points on the 30-year loan, up from 1.7 percent in the previous week. They charged 1.7 percent on 15-year loans, unchanged from the prior week, and 1.3 percent on ARM loans, down from 1.4 percent.
Freddie Mac is a corporation chartered by Congress that buys mortgages from lenders and packages them into securities for investors.
